# GameSurf — August 2002 Italian preview

- Original source: [Robin Hood](https://www.gamesurf.it/anteprime/gioco/robin-hood-c7494)
- Author / publication: Redazione; GameSurf.
- Language / date: Italian; 2002-08-04.
- Access: Full two-page preview retrieved directly, including the closing verdict box
- Checked: 2026-09-09
- Retrieved: 2026-09-09
- Archived copy: lookup failed (archive.org rate limit); not checked
- Format: header notes, original summary, then complete factual notes (commercial preview, not transcribed)

The preview positions Robin Hood as Spellbound’s follow-up to Desperados. It argues that Desperados initially suffered from being dismissed as a Commandos imitation, whereas the new game would attract greater curiosity. The inspected material recounts the outlaw premise and expresses optimism about the setting and production care.

This is prerelease expectation, not a review of the finished game. It complements GameSurf’s later December review, which again stresses looking beyond an initial impression of similarity to Commandos. The preview’s story retelling is not treated as historical scholarship.

## Detailed notes

Page facts: title "Robin Hood" (section: Anteprime, previews); byline "di Redazione"; dated 04 agosto 2002 22:00; game card link "Robin Hood"; retrieved directly from gamesurf.it. Page 1 was retrieved first and page 2 in a second pass (covered below). Beneath the pagination the page shows a boxed closing assessment ("Robin Hood") that appears to be the preview's verdict box. Commercial Italian editorial content, not transcribed. No score is shown on the preview.

Page 1 body, in order:

- Opening: "last season" a title from a young German software house, Spellbound, came out. Because the studio was little known, the game was met with general indifference and in the earliest comments was branded a shameless clone of the first Commandos. By the time people noticed that was not really the case, Commandos 2 was about to arrive with far greater visibility.
- The writer argues Desperados was actually one of the previous year's revelations: first-rate graphics, an original and fascinating setting, and a richness of strategic options "perhaps superior even to" Pyro Studios' more famous series.
- Now "these bold Germans" return with a title that, unlike its predecessor, will be released to great curiosity, because Robin Hood is a legend "we have heard practically forever". Some hold he really existed, others rule it out.
- Story retelling given by the preview (presented as background for the reader): Robin (Hood) of Locksley is a likeable Saxon lad who leaves for the Crusades "of the eleventh century"; after a rather long imprisonment he returns home expecting everything as before, but finds his manor and lands seized by Prince John Lackland (Giovanni Senza Terra), the wicked brother of Richard the Lionheart, who has also gone to the Holy Land. From there begins the romantic story of the bandit who robs the rich to give to the poor, living with his merry band of ragamuffins in the tangled Sherwood forest, slowly reconquering what was taken and becoming a legend more than a hero.
- The writer notes it is hard to say whether any of this is true, but "what counts is the legend"; otherwise, about 1000 years later, a group of young German programmers could never have based a strategy game on it.
- An image table placeholder ("table_img_3" with images 4, 5, 6) follows, then pagination to page 2.

Closing assessment box (shown on the retrieved page under the game name "Robin Hood"): the setting is one that cannot fail to please; the care taken over the title "seems really high" and fun is assured; "a few more months" and we will see whether Desperados will have a little brother worthy of it.

Page 1 contains no description of missions, characters or mechanics; those are on page 2, below.

### Page 2, added from continuation retrieval

Retrieved directly from gamesurf.it on 2026-09-09; same byline and date. Content, in order:

- This time Robin will keep the money rather than give it to the poor: it is needed for King Richard's ransom, and he has "40 (!!!)" missions to do it.
- Everything starts from Sherwood Forest, which contains all that is needed for rest, provisioning and arming the Saxon heroes. The forest lends itself to many rather similar missions, "ambushes in every sauce", perhaps a few too many.
- Variety is not lacking; incursions into enemy territory make up most of the total. Each mission must be prepared in detail; frontal attack, though less so than in Commandos, generally brings disastrous results. Step-by-step advance, eliminating guards and sentries, and infiltrating enemy ranks are the key.
- The classic view cone is present. A system of "stars" appears above the heads of enemies knocked out of action, indicating how long the stunning lasts.
- City missions are "quite effective", 4 in all: York, Lincoln, Derby and Leicester; "it will not be too easy".
- Influence on the plot: almost always a choice between several missions, though overall the game is fairly guided.
- All the historical characters are present: Lady Marian, Friar Tuck ("Frate Tac"), Little John, Will Scarlett "and company". Each is useful in particular missions and choosing the right companions is fundamental; the writer jokes that Will Scarlett "seems to be of really little use... a bit like in the various films".
- The number of men who join depends on success during missions, driven by the player's popularity.
- Graphics: "the perfect demonstration that 2D is not dead"; very high detail, pleasing and careful, with spectacular water effects.
- The closing verdict box repeats the text already recorded above.
